case_study_insert.main_stem: Cobblerow Footwear (CBF) is a private limited company in the footwear retail sector, selling trainers and boots through its website and two outlets and employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2018 by Marcus Cobble, the business operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. CBF plans to invest $480,000 in an automated footwear warehouse and a new online platform, financed by a $180,000 bank overdraft and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $11 a unit and a selling price of $32, and produces 21,000 units a year. CBF faces a product defect rate of 3.8% on returned shoes and rising complaints about delivery damage.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Online Operations Report — Q4 2025: CBF dispatched 6,300 pairs last quarter, with a product defect rate of 3.8% on returns, up from 2.1% a year ago. Damage-in-transit complaints rose to 34 from 18 per month, and average delivery time was 4.6 days. A survey of 650 online shoppers found 57% cared about free delivery and 44% would pay extra for faster shipping. A skills audit shows 8 of 28 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the local college costs $580 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Cobblerow Footwear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Retail Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of CBF's $180,000 bank overdraft. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.40 to $14.23 an hour from April 2026, raising warehouse payroll costs. (3) Leather and synthetic upper input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while online spending on footwear grew 4.8%.

questions.question_text: CBF is funding its $480,000 expansion with a $180,000 bank overdraft and a $300,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for CBF of the share issue compared with the overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue provides $300,000 that does not have to be repaid and carries no regular interest charge, unlike the $180,000 bank overdraft whose cost rises whenever the base rate moves. For a business with fixed costs of $210,000 a year and delivery-damage complaints, this protects cash flow while the automated warehouse and online platform are built, leaving more of the $32 selling price to cover the $11 variable cost and absorb the 11.3% rise in upper-material costs.

Point 2: Equity does not expose CBF to the daily repayment pressure or collateral of an overdraft, so Marcus Cobble's new platform cannot be undermined by a bank recall if sales dip below the 6,300-pair quarterly baseline. Although issuing shares dilutes ownership, it spreads risk among investors rather than concentrating it on one lender and avoids the variable-rate interest exposure created by a 4.75% base rate. That stability suits a flat structure with democratic leadership, where the workforce of 28 needs confidence to invest effort in reducing the 3.8% defect rate while $480,000 is being spent on the new warehouse.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to CBF's expansion financing.

questions.question_text: CBF wants to raise sales through its new online platform. Consider national television advertising, local radio advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should CBF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television could build rapid awareness of the website and the two outlets among shoe buyers nationwide, supporting the 44% of 650 surveyed shoppers who would pay extra for faster shipping. However, airtime is expensive for a firm with $210,000 fixed costs and a $180,000 overdraft, and most viewers will not convert immediately, so much of the spend is wasted relative to the $480,000 expansion budget.

Local radio advertising: Radio is cheaper and can reach drivers near the two outlets with a simple message about the new platform and faster delivery. Its limitations are that audio cannot show the footwear, its reach is narrow compared with a website that sells nationally, and it does little to reassure the 57% of surveyed shoppers who care about free delivery; it also cannot address the 34 damage-in-transit complaints visually.

Social media influencer marketing: Footwear and fitness influencers can model the trainers and boots, demonstrate the unboxing and delivery experience, and link directly to the online platform, reaching the 57% who care about delivery terms and the 44% who would pay for speed. Engagement is measurable against the 6,300-pair baseline and the 34 damage complaints. Drawbacks are that credible influencers charge fees, results develop gradually, and any negative comment about the 3.8% defect rate could spread quickly.

Recommendation: CBF should choose social media influencer marketing, with a small radio reminder in the two outlet towns. It shows the product, sells the delivery proposition and reaches a national online audience at far lower cost than television for a $480,000 expansion partly funded by overdraft. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and radio is rejected as the main channel because it cannot display footwear or drive online traffic effectively. Marcus Cobble should track the 6,300-pair baseline and the 34 complaints before scaling spend.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to CBF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CBF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: CBF's product defect rate is 3.8% and delivery-damage complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for CBF of using democratic leadership with its workforce of 28.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the workforce of 28, especially those packing and dispatching shoes, to suggest how to reduce the 3.8% product defect rate and the 34 damage-in-transit complaints. Because these staff handle every order, their ideas on protective packaging and machine checks are practical, and being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, which lowers error rates and rework in the new automated warehouse.

Point 2: Involvement fits CBF's flat organisational structure and helps staff take ownership of delivery quality, so the 34 complaints can be tackled through team suggestions on packing routines rather than instructions from Marcus Cobble alone. Higher morale also supports the 57% of 650 surveyed shoppers who care about free delivery: careful, engaged staff reduce avoidable returns, protecting the $32 selling price and $21 contribution while 21,000 units a year are dispatched and the $580 training cost per employee is used effectively.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CBF's defects, complaints, structure and output.

questions.question_text: CBF must train 8 of 28 staff who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should CBF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching in the warehouse is specific to CBF's own packing and quality checks, costs no course fees, and keeps the 8 trainees productive through the 6,300-pair quarter. Supervisors can immediately correct the habits behind the 3.8% defect rate and the 34 damage complaints, and align training with the 4.6-day delivery target. The drawbacks are that experienced staff lose time teaching, bad habits may be copied, and no external certificate is awarded.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $580 per employee costs 8 × $580 = $4,640, a small sum beside the $480,000 investment. It supplies structured, certified warehousing and quality skills and removes trainees from distractions, valuable when defects and damage are rising. However, it takes 8 of a workforce of 28 away from the warehouse during a busy quarter, risking slower dispatch and more than 34 complaints, and generic content may not match CBF's exact processes without follow-up coaching on site.

Decision: CBF should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with short certified college modules for senior packers later. It is cheaper, process-specific and avoids worsening the 34 complaints while the flat structure and democratic leadership support peer coaching. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because $4,640 and eight lost shifts would disrupt the 21,000-unit output at a sensitive launch. Marcus Cobble should pilot coaching with one packing team, compare the 3.8% defect rate, and only pay the $580 fee later where certification adds real value.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CBF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of CBF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and process relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CBF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($32 − $11) = $210,000 ÷ $21 = 10,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 10,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $32 − $11 = $21. Answer: contribution per unit is $21.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CBF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 10,000-unit break-even point with output of 21,000 units gives a margin of safety of 11,000 units, showing how far online demand can fall before CBF stops covering its $210,000 fixed costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $21 lets managers test delivery offers: funding free delivery from margin reduces the effective contribution, so they can judge whether the 57% of 650 shoppers who care about free delivery would generate enough extra pairs to compensate.
3. With a $180,000 bank overdraft to service and a $480,000 expansion underway, the $21 contribution and 21,000-unit output show the cash available to reduce the overdraft and phase the automated warehouse spend.
4. Unit cost can be checked as $210,000 ÷ 21,000 = $10 plus $11 variable cost = $21 a pair, letting CBF benchmark whether the 3.8% defect rate and 34 damage complaints are raising costs above target each quarter.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 10,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $21 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 11,000-unit margin of safety against 21,000 output; delivery-offer decisions using $21 contribution; reducing the $180,000 overdraft and funding $480,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $21 against defects and damage.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CBF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CBF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 2.00 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.07 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.71 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $75,000 inventories + $20,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $130,000; 2025 current assets = $95,000 + $25,000 + $25,000 = $145,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 $130,000 ÷ $65,000 = 2.00 and ($130,000 − $75,000) ÷ $65,000 = $55,000 ÷ $65,000 = 0.85. For 2025, $145,000 ÷ $70,000 = 2.07 and ($145,000 − $95,000) ÷ $70,000 = $50,000 ÷ $70,000 = 0.71.

Evaluation: The two measures point in different directions. The first rose slightly from 2.00 to 2.07, but that reflects inventories growing from $75,000 to $95,000 while cash fell from $35,000 to $25,000 and current liabilities rose from $65,000 to $70,000. The stock-free measure fell from 0.85 to 0.71, showing that liquid assets now cover less of the short-term debts. For an online footwear retailer with $210,000 fixed costs, a $180,000 overdraft and a $480,000 warehouse project, that is a real weakness: the business depends more on selling shoes that already show a 3.8% defect rate and 34 damage complaints. Trade receivables rose from $20,000 to $25,000, tying up further cash, so the small improvement in the broader measure is not supported by the quality of the assets.

Conclusion: CBF's financial position has not improved. The broader measure is propped up by stock, while the stock-free measure dropped from 0.85 to 0.71, leaving less headroom to meet bills. CBF should reduce inventory and receivables and protect cash before committing more to the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on the financial position.

questions.question_text: CBF is considering offering free delivery on online orders. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CBF of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Free delivery answers the 57% of 650 surveyed shoppers who care about delivery terms, removing a barrier to purchase on the online platform and supporting the $32 selling price and $21 contribution on each pair. More orders would spread the $210,000 fixed costs over the 21,000-unit base and improve the return on the $480,000 warehouse investment.

Disadvantage: Paying delivery out of margin reduces the $21 contribution on every pair and could be exploited by small, frequent orders, while the 3.8% defect rate and 34 damage complaints already generate avoidable costs. The insert provides no figure for average delivery cost or the sales uplift from free delivery, so the net effect cannot be quantified and the decision must be qualitative. Marcus Cobble should trial free delivery above an order threshold, track the 6,300-pair baseline and the 34 complaints, and review the 44% who would pay extra for speed before extending the offer.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CBF's survey, costs, defects and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in leather and synthetic upper input costs will affect CBF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If CBF's $180,000 bank overdraft is fully drawn, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $180,000 = $1,350 a year (0.0075 × $180,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $210,000, though an overdraft is variable-rate by nature so the cost is immediate. The rise may also make future borrowing dearer and could slightly slow the 4.8% growth in online footwear spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.23 an hour): The workforce of 28 includes hourly-paid warehouse and packing staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 21,000 units ÷ 28 staff = 750 pairs per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; reducing the 3.8% defect rate and training the 8 untrained staff would help sustain it.

Upper-material input costs (11.3%): These feed the $11 variable cost on every pair. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $11 were exposed, 11.3% × $11 = $1.243, about $1.24 a pair, and at 21,000 units that is roughly $26,103 a year (21,000 × $1.243). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $21 contribution on each pair, and the effect repeats with every sale.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in upper-material input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 21,000 pairs and directly erodes the $21 contribution that services the $180,000 overdraft and funds the $480,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,350 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 750 pairs per worker. CBF should cut the 3.8% defect rate and review the $32 price rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to CBF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CBF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
